text: A teal disc on a gray field, with a small dark dot at its center. The ring around it counts out the hold time.
Lock your gaze on the center dot. Do not let your eyes wander. Hold for about fifteen seconds.
Now the teal is gone and only empty gray remains. Keep your eyes where the dot was, and do not blink hard. What do you see on the gray?
A soft rose disc, where the teal used to be. Nothing rose is on the screen.
The cones that drank the teal are tired, so the gray tips toward teal's opposite. You are seeing fatigue, rendered as color. Vision is not recording, it is construction.
A field of slanted bars is drifting. Through this small porthole you only catch the middles of the bars, never their ends.
Watch the drift. Which way does it seem to go? The dim arrow marks the direction you most likely see.
Is that the true direction? Through a slot, countless different motions would look exactly like this. The porthole cannot tell them apart.
Now pull the rim wide. The bar ends come into view, and the bright arrow swings to the real heading.
It was moving that way all along. Through the slot, every direction looked the same. Vision is not recording, it is construction.
Two pale dots, side by side, with a dark gap between them. One lights, then the other, then back. At this slow rhythm you see exactly what is there: two lamps blinking in turn.
Now speed the rhythm up. Watch the gap between the dots.
Keep watching the gap. Is anything moving across it?

One object slides across the gap and back, yet nothing ever travels that space. Both dots only switch on and off in place. Two lamps, two still flashes, and a gap nothing crosses. The motion was yours, built from stillness. Vision is not recording, it is construction.
Rows of light and dark tiles, with thin gray lines between them. Each row is nudged sideways against the one above. Look at the gray lines.
Push the shift further, and keep watching the gray lines.
Now slide the offset back toward zero. Watch the gray lines as the tiles line up.
Zero shift. Look at the gray lines now.
They were dead level and parallel the whole time. Offset tiles and gray mortar made you bend them: the slope was yours. Vision is construction, not a recording.
Fifteen warm-gray tiles flash on, then off, then on again. One of them switches shades every cycle. Study the grid and try to catch which tile it is.
A blank flash sits between every frame. Keep looking. Can you find the tile that changes?
Now close the blank. With the two frames butting straight together, watch the grid.

There it is, marked. The blank wiped the signal that would have pulled your eye to it, and you never stored the scene to compare. Even a whole tile changing in plain sight can go unseen. Vision is construction, not a recording.
A checkerboard with a soft shadow across it. Square A sits on the lit half. Square B sits inside the shadow.
Compare the two. Which looks lighter, A or B?
Now the readout. It measures the light each square sends to your eye: the same for both. Same gray, yet they refuse to look alike.
Now drag the shadow off B. Watch the two squares, and the readout.
The illusion drops. They were always the same gray. Your visual system discounted the shadow and reported the surface, not the light. Vision is construction, not a recording.
One field, split down the middle. Compare the left half with the right. Is one of them lighter?
Now look only at the seam. A soft cusp ramps from light on the left to dark on the right, and nothing else lies between the halves.
Slide an ink bar across the seam to hide the cusp. Watch the two halves.
Covered, the two halves match: one flat gray. They always were. You read the little edge and repainted the whole surface to match. Vision is construction, not a recording.
Two pale discs, one on the left, one on the right. Compare their sizes. Do they match?
Now look at their neighbors. The left disc sits inside a ring of large circles; the right one inside a ring of small ones.
Watch the centers as the surrounding rings even out. Nothing about the two discs is changing. Only their context is.
Rings matched. Compare the two centers again.

They were the same size all along, and the readout said so. Size is judged against the neighbors, not measured: the same disc shrinks beside giants and swells beside dwarves. Vision is construction, not a recording.
Eight points joined by twelve lines, seen square on. Hold that view for a moment.
Now turn it. Watch what happens to the box.
From here the points hang at unrelated depths. This loose cloud is one scene that fits the flat image, and endless other arrangements fit it just as well. The picture alone cannot tell them apart.
Return to the one viewpoint where the points align. What do you see?

A cube, at once: your visual system commits to the simplest cause. But there was never a cube. The flat image fit endless scenes, and you saw the simplest. Vision is not recording, it is construction.
Three pale discs, each with a wedge bitten out of its rim. Look at the space in the middle, between them.
Keep your eyes on the middle as the wedges swing around to face it.
Stay on the middle. What do you see there?
A bright triangle with crisp edges, and none of it is drawn. Only three notched discs exist. The surface, the brightness, the edges: you supplied them all. Vision is construction, not a recording.
A spiral of cream arms on a dark field, with a small dot at the center. Keep your eyes on that dot for the whole walk.
Now it spins. Hold your gaze on the center and let it run.
Stay on the dot. Give it a slow count of twenty.
Stopped. The spiral is dead still. Keep your eyes on the dot. What does it do?

It drifts the other way, drawing inward, though nothing on the screen is moving. The spinning tired your outward-motion detectors, and their silence reads as motion. Vision is not recording, it is construction.
Three amber dots sit out toward the edges over a still mask, bright and obvious. Keep your eyes on the center cross.
Now the mask begins to turn. Hold your gaze on the cross. Do not chase the dots.
Keep fixating the center. Notice the dots at the edge of your vision.
Now the mask stops. Keep watching the dots.

The dots dropped out, and they return all at once, exactly where they always were. They never dimmed and never moved. Salience is no guarantee of being seen. Motion captured the system and the rest dropped out. Vision is not a recording, it is construction.
Two horizontal shafts, one above the other, with fins at their ends. Which shaft is longer?
Now check the readout. It gives the length of each shaft in pixels.
Now drag the fins flat. Watch the two shafts.
Flat. The shafts line up exactly, because they were always the same length. The fins were never measuring anything. Your visual system was.

Outward fins read as a near corner and stretch a line; inward fins read as a far corner and shrink it. Nothing on the screen changed length. Only the corners you inferred. Vision is construction, not a recording.
Two pale horizontal bars, upper and lower, framed by a pair of rails that converge toward the top like a road running into the distance.
Compare the two bars. Which looks longer?
Now watch the bars as the rails straighten out.
Rails gone. Look at the bars again, and at the readout: both have measured the same width the entire time.
The converging lines read as depth, so the upper bar must be farther, so your visual system enlarged it to keep the world constant. Vision is construction, not a recording.
A regular lattice of gray bars with a pale disc at every crossing. Every disc is the same flat gray. Hold still and take in the whole field.
Now let your eyes drift around the grid. Watch the crossings.
Fix on one single crossing and stare at it.

Dark dots shimmered at the crossings you were not looking at, and vanished where you stared. They are not on the page. Your retina overshoots into phantom darkness where bright neighbors crowd a crossing. Vision is construction, not a recording.
A soft ring sits out in your periphery and a small cross marks the center. Fix your gaze on that cross and do not let your eyes wander.
Hold steady. Keep staring straight at the cross and let the ring stay at the corner of your vision. Do not chase it.
Keep waiting, without moving your eyes. What happens to the ring?
Now flick your eyes. The ring is back at full strength: it never left the screen. Steady, unchanging input stops being reported. Vision is not recording, it is construction.
